steps.tx: During the fourth and fifth weeks, the developing head and neck display six pairs of rounded mesenchymal swellings designated **pharyngeal arches**, numbered one through six (arch five regressing rapidly). Each arch consists of a mesenchymal core derived from paraxial mesoderm and neural crest, bounded externally by ectodermal clefts and internally by endodermal pouches.
steps.say: In weeks four and five, the embryonic neck exhibits rounded mesenchymal bars termed pharyngeal arches, numbered one to six. Each arch contains a core of mesoderm and neural crest, wrapped externally by ectodermal clefts and internally by endodermal pouches.

vis.alt: Pharyngeal arches, skeletal bars, cranial nerve innervation, and muscles
vis.caption: Pharyngeal arch cranial nerves and muscular derivatives. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Every pharyngeal arch receives a dedicated cranial nerve, a skeletal cartilaginous bar, an aortic arch artery, and a muscular primordium. The **first pharyngeal arch** (mandibular arch) is innervated by the mandibular nerve (V3). Its muscular derivatives comprise the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, and tensor veli palatini.
steps.say: Every pharyngeal arch receives a cranial nerve, a skeletal rod, an artery, and a muscular block. The first arch is innervated by the mandibular nerve. It forms the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, and tensor veli palatini.

rows: Stapes, styloid process, lesser horn hyoid
Greater horn and lower body of hyoid

steps.tx: The cartilaginous bar of the first arch is Meckel cartilage, which undergoes endochondral ossification at its dorsal extremity to form the malleus and incus of the middle ear. The **second pharyngeal arch** (hyoid arch) is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII), giving rise to muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior digastric.
steps.say: The first arch Meckel cartilage forms the malleus and incus. The second arch is supplied by the facial nerve and forms the muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and the posterior digastric belly. Its cartilage builds the stapes and styloid process.

right.title: Second Arch Skeletal
points: Lesser horn and upper body of hyoid

steps.tx: The third pharyngeal arch is innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), supplying a single muscle, the stylopharyngeus. Its cartilage forms the greater horn and lower body of the hyoid bone. The fourth arch is innervated by the **superior laryngeal nerve**, while the sixth arch is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
steps.say: The third arch is innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve, supplying only the stylopharyngeus muscle and forming the greater horn of the hyoid bone. The fourth arch is innervated by the superior laryngeal nerve, while the sixth arch is innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

steps.tx: Internally, four pairs of endodermal outpocketings known as pharyngeal pouches develop between the arches. The **first pharyngeal pouch** expands into an elongated tubotympanic recess, whose distal expansion forms the tympanic middle ear cavity and mastoid antrum. The proximal stalk remains narrow to form the pharyngotympanic (Eustachian) tube.
steps.say: Internally, four pairs of endodermal pharyngeal pouches project outward. The first pouch dilates into the tubotympanic recess, whose distal end forms the middle ear cavity and mastoid antrum. Its narrow proximal segment persists as the Eustachian tube.

vis.alt: Pharyngeal pouch 1-4 derivatives: tonsil, parathyroids, thymus
vis.caption: Pharyngeal pouch endocrine and lymphatic organogenesis. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The second pharyngeal pouch is largely obliterated by the expanding palatine tonsil, persisting as the tonsillar fossa and crypts. The third pharyngeal pouch differentiates into two components: the dorsal wing forms the **inferior parathyroid gland**, while the ventral wing migrates into the anterior mediastinum to form the bilateral lobes of the thymus.
steps.say: The second pouch is largely absorbed by the palatine tonsil, leaving the tonsillar crypts. The third pouch divides into two wings: the dorsal wing forms the inferior parathyroid gland, while the ventral wing migrates into the chest to establish the thymus gland.

points: Ventral wing: Bilateral lobes of thymus
Migrates caudally past fourth pouch derivatives
Thymus pulls inferior parathyroid into lower neck

right.title: Fourth Pouch Derivatives

Superior parathyroid remains higher on posterior thyroid

steps.tx: Because the thymus migrates long distances caudally, it drags parathyroid III with it, causing the third pouch derivative to settle below the fourth pouch derivative as the inferior parathyroid. The fourth pharyngeal pouch dorsal wing forms the **superior parathyroid gland**, while its ventral ultimobranchial body fuses with the thyroid gland to contribute calcitonin-secreting parafollicular C cells.
steps.say: Because the thymus journeys far into the chest, it drags parathyroid three along, positioning it lower than parathyroid four as the inferior parathyroid gland. The fourth pouch dorsal wing forms the superior parathyroid, while its ventral body yields calcitonin C cells in the thyroid.

nodes.label: Adult Anatomy: Parathyroid III sits Inferior

steps.tx: Failure of normal pharyngeal pouch and arch differentiation leads to significant clinical syndromes. In **DiGeorge syndrome** (22q11.2 microdeletion), failure of third and fourth pouch organogenesis results in congenital absence of the thymus causing severe T-cell immunodeficiency, alongside parathyroid aplasia triggering neonatal tetany and hypocalcemia.
steps.say: Defective pouch differentiation produces distinct clinical syndromes. In DiGeorge syndrome, agenesis of the third and fourth pouches causes thymic aplasia with severe T-cell immunodeficiency and parathyroid aplasia leading to neonatal hypocalcemia and tetany.
